paragraphs: Self-supervised learning aims to extract useful representations from unlabeled examples so that later tasks need fewer labels. This paper examines methods that push a representation's covariance or correlation matrix toward the identity matrix. The authors identify a problem with these objectives: estimates computed from finite samples can be biased, shifting what the model optimizes when training uses small batches.

Adv-SSL replaces this approach with an adversarial, minimax formulation designed to support unbiased transfer learning. The authors report that it does so without additional cost relative to the biased alternatives they consider. Their contribution combines a training method with theoretical guarantees connecting representation learning to subsequent classification.

The analysis shows that the minimax objective encourages distinct clusters in representation space when sufficiently much unlabeled training data is available. That condition matters: the clustering conclusion depends on adequate upstream data. Experiments report improvements over existing methods across multiple benchmarks, alongside strong classification with few downstream labels. Together, these findings connect a correction to the learning objective with representations that transfer effectively.
neurips-2025-adv-ssl-adversarial-self-su.tldr: Adv-SSL uses adversarial optimization to address biased self-supervised objectives and supports effective transfer with few labels.

paragraphs: Choosing the best option through repeated experiments creates a practical tension: additional observations cost something, but stopping too early can produce a poor recommendation. Traditional best-arm identification methods ask users to specify either a sampling budget or a desired confidence level. This paper proposes expressing the underlying tradeoff directly, rather than requiring practitioners to choose those parameters first.

The proposed objective adds the cost of collecting observations to a penalty for recommending a suboptimal option. The authors study two penalties: the probability of choosing incorrectly and simple regret, which measures how much performance the recommendation loses relative to the best option. These distinguish avoiding mistakes from avoiding costly mistakes.

The paper derives theoretical lower bounds on achievable combined risk and introduces DBCARE, which matches them up to polylogarithmic factors on nearly all problem instances. Simulations compare it with fixed-budget and fixed-confidence algorithms, illustrating shortcomings of those approaches under the new objective. The contribution is a framework for deciding how much learning is economically worthwhile, together with an algorithm supported by near-matching guarantees.
neurips-2025-balancing-performance-and-c.tldr: DBCARE balances sampling costs against recommendation quality, approaching theoretical risk limits on nearly all problem instances.

paragraphs: Speech and language models can help study language processing by predicting brain responses to language. Existing methods often depend heavily on the particular participant and the amount of brain data collected from that person. This makes it difficult to transfer a model to someone new or use it to investigate patterns across a population.

The authors fine-tune pretrained speech language models to predict fMRI responses from several participants jointly. This shared training aims to retain alignment with individual brains while learning representations that generalize between people. It moves the learning process beyond fitting a separate participant's responses in isolation.

The resulting models need five times less fMRI data to predict responses from new participants, show up to a 50% increase in overall brain alignment, and generalize strongly to unseen datasets. They also improve on downstream semantic tasks. That last finding suggests that learning from multiple participants' brain responses can improve semantic representations as well as brain prediction. The evidence therefore supports benefits in both directions: better tools for neuroscience and useful training signals for AI.
neurips-2025-brain-tuning-improves-gener.tldr: Training speech models jointly on multiple participants' brain responses improves brain alignment, data efficiency, and semantic task performance.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks often represent pairs of nodes to predict links, yet much of their theoretical analysis concerns entire graphs. These are different questions: distinguishing two graphs does not directly explain how well a model distinguishes relationships within them. This paper develops a theoretical account specifically for representations of node pairs.

Its central contribution is a unifying framework, called the k_phi–k_rho–m framework, that covers existing message-passing link models. The authors use it to organize methods into an expressiveness hierarchy and provide tools for analyzing future architectures. They also introduce a synthetic benchmark designed specifically to test link-level expressiveness.

The practical analysis connects model expressiveness to graph symmetry, using a metric that measures how difficult links are to distinguish. More expressive models can perform worse on standard benchmarks, but significantly outperform simpler models as symmetry increases in the studied settings. The implication is that theoretical power becomes valuable when the data demands it. Model selection should therefore consider graph structure rather than assume the most expressive architecture will always perform best.
neurips-2025-bridging-theory-and-practic.tldr: A link-level expressiveness framework shows why more powerful graph models become especially useful as graph symmetry increases.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that the markets supplying information to AI systems need structural change. Journalists, researchers, creative professionals, and smaller organizations contribute information with economic value, but the authors contend that these producers need collective representation to negotiate reasonable terms and compensation with AI product builders.

The proposal is to let information producers appoint representatives who bargain on their behalf. Making this workable requires both technical infrastructure and policy support. The paper identifies explainable estimates of data value and federated data management as useful technical directions, alongside trusted intermediary organizations representing groups such as guilds or syndicates.

The authors argue that failing to establish collective bargaining would intensify information-market failures and concentrate capital. They also warn of a possible collapse in the shared information resources on which AI depends. These are arguments about institutional risks and opportunities, rather than experimentally established outcomes. The paper presents coalition-based actions intended to support bargaining and argues that such arrangements can help create market conditions needed for socially beneficial AI.
neurips-2025-collective-bargaining-in-th.tldr: This position paper advocates collective bargaining for information producers to improve compensation and counter AI-driven concentration of power.

paragraphs: Extracting individual motor-unit activity from muscle recordings can provide detailed signals for controlling assistive devices. However, existing decomposition algorithms can be slow and inconsistent. MUelim addresses this computational bottleneck in high-density electromyography, aiming to make those signals useful for real-time, intention-driven neuroprosthetic control.

The algorithm augments recordings through an extend-lag procedure to make underlying sources easier to separate. It then uses approximate joint diagonalization and a subtractive process to identify and refine candidate sources. Repeatedly eliminating redundant or noisy candidates reduces computational complexity while maintaining accurate decomposition.

Tests use simulated recordings and physiological data from six healthy participants performing ramp and maximum voluntary contractions. MUelim achieves up to a 36-fold speed increase over existing leading methods while extracting a similar number of sources with high signal-to-noise ratios. A clinical demonstration involves one person with spinal cord injury controlling an EMG-driven neuroprosthesis. A spiking neural network decodes the extracted motor-unit activity to trigger electrical stimulation for hand movements. This demonstrates real-time functional use and supports the method's potential for nuanced assistive control.
neurips-2025-decomposing-motor-units-thr.tldr: MUelim accelerates motor-unit extraction and demonstrates real-time intention decoding for an assistive neuroprosthesis.

paragraphs: One proposed explanation for diffusion models' generalization is that they adapt to low-dimensional structure hidden within complex data. Under the manifold hypothesis, meaningful examples occupy a structured region with fewer effective dimensions than their full representation suggests. This paper investigates a possible mechanism connecting that geometry to the score-matching objective used to train diffusion models.

The authors study what happens when solutions minimizing the empirical score-matching objective are smoothed. Their theoretical and empirical results show that smoothing the score function, equivalently smoothing in the log-density domain, produces smoothing along directions tangent to the data manifold. The smoothing therefore responds to the geometry of the data.

The paper also shows that selecting an appropriate smoothing can control the manifold along which the diffusion model generalizes. This links the choice of smoothing to the structure of the resulting generalization. The findings provide evidence for the geometric explanation of diffusion performance and identify a concrete mechanism through which score matching could support it, rather than establishing that this mechanism explains every aspect of diffusion models' success.
neurips-2025-diffusion-models-and-the-ma.tldr: Theoretical and empirical results show how score smoothing can adapt diffusion-model generalization to low-dimensional data geometry.

paragraphs: Process reward models evaluate intermediate reasoning steps, giving a model guidance before it reaches a final answer. Extending them to multimodal reasoning is difficult because tasks vary widely and training datasets differ in quality. A large training collection can therefore contain uneven reasoning signals, while still failing to cover the kinds of tasks encountered at evaluation time.

DreamPRM addresses this through two connected optimization levels. The lower level fine-tunes a process reward model on multiple datasets, assigning different weights to their domains. The upper level evaluates that model on a separate meta-learning dataset and uses the feedback to update the weights. This makes the influence of each domain responsive to how well the trained evaluator generalizes.

Experiments across mathematical and general multimodal reasoning report consistent improvements when DreamPRM supports additional computation at test time. Its weighting strategy outperforms the compared data-selection methods and produces larger accuracy gains than existing test-time scaling approaches. Using o4-mini, the reported MathVista top-1 accuracy reaches 85.2%. These findings support treating training-data balance as a central part of building a useful multimodal reasoning evaluator.
neurips-2025-dreamprm-domain-reweighted-.tldr: DreamPRM learns how much to weight each training domain, improving process reward models for multimodal reasoning.

paragraphs: First-person video captures interactions in a three-dimensional world, but video-language pretraining often relies on text and two-dimensional visual cues. Those signals provide descriptions and image locations without directly supplying depth. EgoDTM adds explicit depth-oriented supervision to help a video model learn spatial information alongside the correspondence between videos and language.

The approach combines large-scale 3D-aware video pretraining with video-text contrastive learning. A lightweight decoder learns from pseudo depth maps produced by depth estimation models. These are estimated depth signals, which supply a spatial training target without being described as directly measured depth. The authors also combine foundation models to enrich short captions with visual information about hands and objects.

Together, the depth maps and expanded captions provide complementary supervision for understanding interactions from the wearer's viewpoint. Experiments report superior performance across diverse downstream tasks, which the authors interpret as evidence of stronger 3D-aware visual understanding. The contribution is a pretraining approach that joins spatial and linguistic learning, using generated depth targets and richer descriptions to make first-person video representations more informative.
neurips-2025-egodtm-towards-3d-aware-ego.tldr: EgoDTM combines estimated depth and enriched captions to improve spatial understanding in first-person video-language models.

paragraphs: Concept-based explanations try to describe a neural network's decisions using recognizable patterns. However, explanations added after training do not always faithfully reflect the model's actual computations. Existing approaches can also impose restrictive expectations, such as assuming concepts belong to individual classes, occupy small image regions, or match concepts humans already anticipate.

FaCT introduces a model whose concept explanations are built into its mechanism. Concepts can be shared across classes, and their contributions to a class score can be traced from any layer. The model also supports tracing those concepts back to visualizations of the input. This connects what a concept looks like with how it contributes to a decision.

The authors additionally introduce C²-Score, a concept-consistency measure that uses foundation models to evaluate concept-based methods. Compared with prior work, they report more consistent concepts quantitatively and concepts that users judge more interpretable, while preserving competitive ImageNet performance. These findings address distinct requirements: an explanation should follow the model's computation, present coherent concepts, and remain understandable to people without giving up useful predictive performance.
neurips-2025-fact-faithful-concept-trace.tldr: FaCT builds traceable concept explanations into a neural network while retaining competitive image-classification performance.

paragraphs: Foundation models have become useful across specialized imaging fields, but evaluating them for Mars science has lacked a common framework. Without standardized tasks and datasets, it is harder to compare approaches systematically or assess whether existing pretrained models transfer effectively. Mars-Bench provides a shared evaluation resource for this setting.

The benchmark contains 20 datasets covering both orbital and surface imagery. Tasks include image classification, segmentation, and object detection, with geological targets such as craters, cones, boulders, and frost. These tasks examine different capabilities: recognizing image content, identifying regions, and locating objects. The authors provide ready-to-use datasets and baseline evaluations.

The evaluated models include systems pretrained on natural images, Earth satellite imagery, and leading vision-language models. Across the analyses, the results suggest that Mars-specific foundation models may have advantages over general-domain models. That finding motivates further investigation of pretraining adapted to Martian data; it does not establish that specialization will always win. The benchmark's broader contribution is a consistent basis for developing and comparing models across multiple Mars-science tasks.
neurips-2025-mars-bench-a-benchmark-for-.tldr: Mars-Bench standardizes evaluation across 20 Mars-imagery datasets and motivates further study of Mars-specific pretraining.

paragraphs: Differentiable logic gate networks aim to make image classification efficient by learning networks of logic gates. Their training process, however, can take days or weeks even on relatively simple benchmarks. They also face a mismatch between the form used during training and the discrete gates used at inference, producing a drop in predictive performance.

The paper addresses this discretization gap by adding Gumbel noise during training and using a straight-through estimator. The estimator allows learning to proceed through choices that would otherwise obstruct ordinary gradient-based updates. The authors theoretically explain the resulting improvement through implicit Hessian regularization, connecting the training modification to better convergence properties.

The reported networks train 4.5 times faster in wall-clock time, reduce the discretization gap by 98%, and eliminate unused gates in the evaluated setting. These results address both training efficiency and how effectively the learned network survives conversion to its inference form. Despite the title's wording, the stated numerical result is a substantial reduction in the performance gap, alongside complete removal of unused gates in the reported experiments.
neurips-2025-mind-the-gap-removing-the-d.tldr: Noise-based training accelerates logic gate networks and reduces their training-to-inference performance gap by 98%.

paragraphs: Walking assistance for people with blindness or low vision requires understanding more than isolated objects. A system must interpret complex surroundings, navigation risks, and accessibility-relevant landmarks. The authors build mmWalk, a simulated dataset designed around these needs, with multiple views and sensing modalities supporting a broader picture of outdoor scenes.

The dataset includes 120 manually controlled walking trajectories and 62,000 synchronized frames, containing more than 559,000 panoramic images across color, depth, and semantic modalities. Each trajectory includes unusual outdoor situations and accessibility-specific landmarks. The accompanying mmWalkVQA benchmark supplies more than 69,000 visual question-answer examples across nine categories focused on safe and informed walking.

Evaluations find that leading vision-language models struggle with the benchmark's risk assessment and navigation tasks when given no examples or only a few examples. The authors also test a model fine-tuned on mmWalk using real-world datasets and report evidence of the dataset's usefulness. The contribution combines targeted training material with an evaluation that exposes weaknesses relevant to walking assistance, while keeping the distinction between simulated data and real-world validation explicit.
neurips-2025-mmwalk-towards-multi-modal-.tldr: mmWalk provides simulated multimodal walking data and a question-answer benchmark that reveals navigation weaknesses in vision-language models.

paragraphs: Shared representation spaces can connect text, images, and audio, but human motion sequences remain less integrated. MotionBind adds motion to the LanguageBind embedding space so that movements can be connected with descriptions, visual context, and sound. This matters because each modality supplies a different part of an action's meaning.

Its first component, the Multi-Scale Temporal Motion Transformer, converts motion sequences into semantic representations. Training uses several kinds of paired information: motion and text from HumanML3D and KIT-ML, motion and rendered video from AMASS, and motion-video-audio examples from AIST++. These complementary signals connect motion to the existing multimodal space rather than relying on descriptions alone.

The second component, a retrieval-augmented latent diffusion model called REALM, generates motion conditioned on multiple modalities. Together, the components support both understanding and producing movement. The authors report state-of-the-art or competitive results across motion reconstruction, cross-modal retrieval, zero-shot action recognition, and text-to-motion generation. The qualification matters: the abstract reports a mixture of leading and competitive performance, supporting the architecture's breadth across tasks rather than uniform dominance on every benchmark.
neurips-2025-motionbind-multi-modal-huma.tldr: MotionBind connects human motion with text, video, and audio to support retrieval, recognition, reconstruction, and generation.

paragraphs: Multimodal contrastive learning trains representations by connecting information across modalities. A representation vector may contain many coordinates, but the shared information in the underlying data can have far fewer effective dimensions. This paper studies whether contrastive learning can adapt to that smaller structure, rather than simply using the dimensionality chosen by the model designer.

The theoretical analysis goes beyond linear representations and specific data distributions. It finds that optimizing the temperature enables multimodal contrastive learning both to maximize mutual information between modalities and to adapt to intrinsic data dimensions. These are related but distinct properties: retaining shared information does not by itself describe how compactly that information is represented.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate representations that are informative and low-dimensional, connecting the theoretical account to observed learning behavior. The role of temperature optimization is central to the stated result, so the conclusion should not be read as an unconditional property of every contrastive setup. The work helps explain how a large representation space can accommodate learned structure whose effective dimensionality is substantially smaller.
neurips-2025-multi-modal-contrastive-lea.tldr: With temperature optimization, multimodal contrastive learning can preserve shared information while adapting to its lower intrinsic dimensionality.

paragraphs: Open-world driving perception must handle unfamiliar objects, unusual situations, and changes in sensing conditions. The authors argue that existing 3D perception benchmarks do not comprehensively evaluate this combination. OpenAD addresses that gap by bringing corner-case objects from multiple autonomous-driving datasets into a common benchmark for three-dimensional detection.

The benchmark uses a discovery and annotation pipeline incorporating a multimodal large language model. It produces annotations in a unified format across five driving-perception datasets and 2,000 scenarios. The authors also develop evaluation methods and assess a range of open-world and specialized models operating in two and three dimensions.

Beyond the benchmark, the paper introduces a vision-centric baseline for open-world 3D detection. It also proposes an ensemble combining general and specialized models to address the low precision of existing open-world methods on OpenAD. The contribution therefore includes both a way to measure difficult perception cases and an approach intended to improve handling of them. An online challenge and released evaluation tools support continued comparison of methods under this shared evaluation setting.
neurips-2025-openad-open-world-autonomou.tldr: OpenAD unifies unusual driving scenarios for evaluating open-world 3D detection and introduces baseline and ensemble approaches.

paragraphs: Using graph machine learning on a relational database requires deciding how to turn tables and relationships into a graph. Rows can become nodes and foreign-key relationships can become edges, but many graph constructions are possible. The paper shows that this modeling choice matters: the best-performing construction can improve predictive performance by up to 10% over a common heuristic.

RDB2G-Bench makes automatic selection of graph constructions easier to study. It covers five real-world relational databases and 12 predictive tasks, with approximately 50,000 pairs linking graph models to measured performance. Precomputing these results lets researchers evaluate selection methods without repeatedly training graph neural networks for every candidate.

Using this resource, the authors benchmark ten automatic modeling methods about 380 times faster than evaluation performed on demand. Their analysis also identifies structural patterns associated with effective graph models and draws practical implications for graph construction. The benchmark turns an expensive design search into a more accessible, reproducible evaluation problem, while emphasizing that the default conversion from database to graph can leave meaningful predictive gains unrealized.
neurips-2025-rdb2g-bench-a-comprehensive.tldr: RDB2G-Bench accelerates evaluation of methods that choose effective graph representations for relational-database prediction tasks.

paragraphs: Chemical reaction predictors should respond to molecular structure rather than arbitrary choices about how atoms or molecules are ordered in the input. Existing models can be sensitive to those orderings and can also inadequately represent interactions between molecular substructures. ReaDISH addresses both issues by combining order-independent representations with explicit interaction modeling.

Its symmetric difference shingle encoding compares sets of molecular substructural pieces to capture changes specific to a reaction. Because the representation is built to be permutation invariant, reordering the input does not change the encoded representation. A second mechanism, geometry-structure interaction attention, models relationships between shingles both within a molecule and across molecules.

These components serve complementary purposes: the encoding removes an irrelevant source of variation, while attention represents interactions relevant to reactivity. Experiments report improved reaction prediction across diverse benchmarks. Under permutation perturbations, the authors report an average 8.76% improvement in R², supporting enhanced robustness to reordered inputs. The findings connect representation design with more consistent predictions and improved benchmark performance, addressing the two weaknesses that motivate the method.
neurips-2025-reaction-prediction-via-int.tldr: ReaDISH combines order-invariant molecular encoding with interaction attention to improve reaction prediction and robustness to input reordering.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how little training data reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can use while still improving mathematical reasoning. The authors identify a single example that, when used to train Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, raises MATH500 performance from 36.0% to 73.6%. Average performance across six mathematics benchmarks rises from 17.6% to 35.7%.

Those results approximately match training on a 1,200-example DeepScaleR subset containing that example; using two examples slightly improves on them. The authors also observe substantial gains across other models, reinforcement-learning algorithms, and mathematical examples. They explicitly separate some gains from format correction, reporting improvements beyond changes in how answers are presented.

The analysis finds generalization across mathematical categories, more frequent self-reflection, and continued test improvement after training accuracy saturates. The authors call the latter post-saturation generalization. They attribute effectiveness primarily to the policy-gradient loss and identify exploration as critical, including appropriately weighted entropy loss. These findings show that very small training sets can produce substantial gains in the studied settings and motivate closer examination of what reinforcement learning changes in an already pretrained model.
neurips-2025-reinforcement-learning-for-.tldr: Reinforcement learning on a single mathematical example can substantially improve reasoning benchmarks, with exploration playing a critical role.

paragraphs: A cache has limited space, so it must choose what to retain as requests arrive. Predictions can improve those choices, but a prediction-guided algorithm may perform poorly when its advice is unreliable. This paper addresses the challenge of adding worst-case protection while preserving the best-case benefit of accurate predictions.

The proposed Guard framework applies to a broad class of learning-augmented caching algorithms. It preserves 1-consistency, the ideal guarantee associated with correct predictions, while providing a robustness bound of 2H_{k-1} + 2. Here, the bound depends on cache size through a harmonic-number expression. The authors describe this as the best-known consistency–robustness tradeoff.

Guard adds only constant computational overhead per request, so it maintains the original time complexity of the underlying algorithm. This is central to its contribution because earlier robustification approaches either weakened consistency or introduced excessive computation. Experiments across multiple real-world datasets and prediction models support its practical effectiveness. The result is a lightweight way to retain the advantages of prediction-based caching while placing a theoretical bound on behavior when predictions are unreliable.
neurips-2025-robustifying-learning-augme.tldr: Guard adds robustness guarantees to prediction-guided caching while preserving 1-consistency and constant additional work per request.

paragraphs: Predictions can change the outcomes they are intended to forecast when people or institutions act on them. This feedback is called performativity and arises in settings such as policymaking and economics. The paper develops statistical inference for this situation, where evaluating uncertainty must account for the interaction between a prediction-informed decision and its target.

The first contribution is a central limit theorem for estimation in the performative setting. This provides a foundation for familiar inferential tasks, including confidence intervals and hypothesis tests. The goal extends beyond selecting a policy or producing a prediction to quantifying uncertainty about the parameters of interest.

The authors then use the theorem to develop prediction-powered inference under performativity. Their approach yields more precise parameter estimates and tighter confidence regions, and numerical experiments validate the framework's effectiveness. These findings connect a theoretical description of estimation uncertainty with a method for improving statistical precision. The work establishes an end-to-end framework for inference in a setting where decisions influence the data-generating outcomes that subsequent analysis seeks to understand.
neurips-2025-statistical-inference-under.tldr: A new inference framework supports uncertainty estimates when prediction-informed decisions change the outcomes being predicted.

paragraphs: Event-based cameras offer high temporal resolution, a broad dynamic range, and low power consumption, but training data remains a bottleneck. Real recordings are scarce, while synthetic pipelines can generate large event streams that are expensive to store and move. V2V changes the data-generation process to make larger-scale event-vision training practical.

The method converts conventional video frames directly into event-based voxel grids. By skipping the intermediate event stream, it avoids a storage-intensive stage of existing pipelines. The authors report a 150-fold reduction in storage requirements. V2V also supports changing simulation parameters on the fly, providing variation intended to improve model robustness.

Using this efficiency, the authors train several architectures for video reconstruction and optical-flow estimation on 10,000 videos totaling 52 hours. They describe this training collection as an order of magnitude larger than existing event datasets and report substantial improvements. The contribution connects a change in data representation with greater training scale: reducing storage and input/output burdens makes a broader collection of conventional videos usable for event-based learning.
neurips-2025-v2v-scaling-event-based-vis.tldr: V2V converts video directly into event voxel grids, cutting storage requirements 150-fold and enabling larger-scale training.

paragraphs: A generated video can look realistic while depicting motion or interactions that violate intuitive physics. The authors find that text-to-video diffusion models contain some physics-relevant information, but their representations lag behind those of recent self-supervised video-understanding models. VideoREPA aims to transfer that stronger understanding into an already pretrained video generator.

The method aligns relationships between tokens using a Token Relation Distillation loss. Its guidance spans space and time, encouraging the generator to learn relational structure from a video-understanding foundation model. The authors emphasize that this soft guidance is suitable for fine-tuning powerful pretrained text-to-video systems, distinguishing it from earlier representation-alignment approaches.

Experiments using CogVideoX report substantial improvements in physical commonsense and relevant benchmark performance, alongside examples of videos that better follow intuitive physics. The findings support relational alignment as a way to improve physical plausibility through knowledge transfer. The demonstrated benefit concerns the evaluated generator and settings: the contribution is an effective fine-tuning framework for injecting physics-relevant understanding, rather than a guarantee that generated videos always obey physical laws.
neurips-2025-videorepa-learning-physics-.tldr: VideoREPA transfers relational knowledge from video-understanding models to improve the physical plausibility of generated videos.

paragraphs: Visual prompt tuning adapts a pretrained model by learning a small set of prompts while leaving the main network fixed. This reduces the resources needed for adaptation, but existing methods can struggle to specialize prompts or enrich the available representations. The authors find these problems especially pronounced with self-supervised backbones, difficult tasks, and limited training data.

VIPAMIN changes how the visual prompts are initialized. It first aligns them with semantically informative regions of the embedding space. It also introduces representational directions beyond the pretrained subspace, combining useful existing structure with an expansion of the space available for adaptation. These two operations address prompt relevance and representational variety together.

The initialization requires only one forward pass and lightweight operations. Across diverse tasks and dataset sizes, the authors report consistent performance improvements and a new state of the art in visual prompt tuning. This supports initialization as a meaningful part of adaptation: choosing where prompts begin can improve their usefulness even when the backbone remains frozen. The low initialization cost makes the approach consistent with prompt tuning's resource-efficient motivation.
neurips-2025-vipamin-visual-prompt-initi.tldr: VIPAMIN improves visual prompt tuning by initializing prompts with informative embeddings and new representational directions.

paragraphs: Adding multiple language-model agents often produces only small benchmark gains, motivating a closer look at how collaboration fails. This paper introduces MAST-Data, a collection of more than 1,600 annotated execution traces from seven multi-agent frameworks. The traces support analysis of failure dynamics across a system's activity rather than only its final answer.

The authors develop the Multi-Agent System Failure Taxonomy through expert-guided analysis of 150 traces. It identifies 14 failure modes grouped into system design, inter-agent misalignment, and task verification. Human annotators achieve agreement of κ = 0.88. An additional language-model judging pipeline agrees strongly with human annotations, making larger-scale labeling more practical.

The taxonomy and dataset are used to examine failures across several model families and coding, mathematics, and general-agent tasks. The analysis identifies room for improvement through better system design and argues that the observed failures require more sophisticated solutions. By releasing the traces, taxonomy, and annotator, the paper provides a shared vocabulary and evaluation resource for investigating coordination problems and guiding future multi-agent development.
neurips-2025-why-do-multi-agent-llm-syst.tldr: MAST categorizes multi-agent failures using annotated traces, creating a systematic basis for diagnosing and improving LLM collaboration.
